clue.text: Cut tours to record company

indicators.note: tours means goes round, so the word for cut is wrapped around the next piece

parts.note: grass that has been cut is mown
taken as written

explanation.surface: A record label slashes its concert tours to save money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tours' looks like a noun about concerts, but it is the verb meaning goes round.
explanation.definitionFit: Motown is the famous Detroit soul label founded by Berry Gordy.

clue.text: Quietly, say, raised drink twice

indicators.note: twice says the upturned drink appears two times in a row
in a down clue raised means the word is written upwards, so read backwards

parts.note: rum is a spirit drink
the same spirit drink, rum, taken a second time

explanation.surface: Someone quietly mentions they have lifted their glass for a second round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' turns RUM upside down in this down entry, giving MUR, and 'twice' repeats it.
explanation.definitionFit: To murmur is to utter words softly, under one's breath.

clue.text: With receipts, banks show favouritism

parts.note: the take is the money received, the takings
the banks of a river are its sides

explanation.surface: A financial report on how banks treat their receipts, accused of bias.
explanation.definitionFit: To take sides is to back one party in a dispute rather than stay neutral.

clue.text: It should sanitise Wuhan pigs, conceivably

parts.note: read the answer as wordplay: WASHING UP made liquid, that is jumbled, gives the letters of Wuhan pigs

explanation.surface: A topical joke about a cleaning product disinfecting livestock from the Chinese city.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue, flagged by 'conceivably': in the answer, LIQUID works as an anagram signal applied to WASHING UP, and the result is WUHAN PIGS.
explanation.definitionFit: Washing-up liquid is the detergent used to clean dishes, so it is meant to make them hygienic.

clue.text: Incorporating one act, 'Play That Goes Wrong' is unusual

indicators.note: something that goes wrong falls into disorder, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
one is I in Roman numerals
taken as written

explanation.surface: A theatre note: the farce The Play That Goes Wrong, given a single act, is out of the ordinary.
explanation.walkthrough: The Play That Goes Wrong is a real West End comedy. 'Incorporating' brings I and ACT into PLAY, and the whole lot is shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: Atypical means not typical, departing from the norm.

clue.text: Spell focus for 'Mastermind'

indicators.note: the focus of a word is its centre, so the middle four letters are taken

explanation.surface: A quiz contestant's specialist subject on the TV show Mastermind.
explanation.walkthrough: Mastermind is a long-running British TV quiz with a famous black chair and specialist subjects.
explanation.definitionFit: A spell and a term both mean a fixed period of time, as in a term in office.

clue.text: Little dash, perhaps, that could give spice to man eating fish

definitions.text: Little dash, perhaps, that could give spice to man eating fish

parts.words: Little dash, perhaps, that could give spice to man eating fish
parts.note: a hyphen is a small dash; adding one turns a man who is eating fish into a fearsome man-eating fish

explanation.surface: A cook's tip for perking up a fish supper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dash' and 'spice' suggest cooking, but the dash is the hyphen in man-eating.
explanation.definitionFit: A hyphen or dash is one of the symbols used to structure written text.

clue.text: After prison, Oscar will be part of orchestra

indicators.note: After says the next letter comes after the prison word

parts.note: a cell is a room in a prison
Oscar is O in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A man called Oscar, released from jail, joins an orchestra.
explanation.definitionFit: The cello is a stringed instrument in the orchestra's string section.

clue.text: Take a chance here — slice of sausage v salami rolls

indicators.note: rolls says the hidden letters are read backwards
a slice of something is a piece cut from inside it, so the letters are taken from within these words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A deli contest: sausage versus salami, sliced and rolled.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft put 'slice' in the definition; 'slice of' is the hiding signal, and 'Take a chance here' alone is the definition. 'rolls' reverses the hidden SAGEVSAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Las Vegas is the Nevada gambling city, where people take chances at casinos.

clue.text: Dashing to have brief smooch in Royal Albert Hall

indicators.note: in says the shortened kiss sits inside the hall letters

parts.note: RAH is the abbreviation for the Royal Albert Hall, a London concert venue

indicators.note: brief means cut short, so the last letter goes

parts.note: a smooch is a kiss

explanation.surface: A daring couple steal a quick kiss at a London concert hall.
explanation.definitionFit: Rakish means stylishly jaunty and devil-may-care, much like dashing.

clue.text: Lines in river catching shellfish? On the contrary

indicators.note: catching means holding inside, so one piece goes within another
this reverses the stated roles, so the shellfish catches the river rather than the other way round

parts.note: winkles are small edible sea snails

explanation.surface: Fishing lines dropped in a river to catch shellfish.
explanation.walkthrough: As written, the river catches the shellfish; 'On the contrary' flips that, so R goes inside WINKLES.
explanation.definitionFit: Wrinkles are creases or lines in the skin.

clue.text: Guys with no sex appeal turning intimate

parts.note: guys are men

indicators.note: turning means turned round, so these letters are read backwards

parts.note: taken as written
IT is old slang for sex appeal

explanation.surface: Unattractive men are becoming close friends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'intimate' looks like an adjective but is the verb, to hint. 'turning' reverses NO IT to TION.
explanation.definitionFit: To intimate is to suggest or hint; to mention is to refer to briefly.

clue.text: Missing clothes apparently mismatched

definitions.meaning: read playfully, it means without a suit

explanation.surface: Someone who has lost their clothes looks oddly put together.
explanation.definitionFit: Unsuited describes people or things ill-matched or not compatible.

clue.text: Pet butterfly?

explanation.definitionFit: To stroke is to caress; butterfly is one example of a swimming stroke.

clue.text: Steal album to look up articles in French and German

indicators.note: in a down clue looking up means read upwards, so the letters go backwards

parts.note: LP is a long-playing record album
un is the French indefinite article
der is a German definite article

explanation.surface: Someone pinches a record to read up on European grammar.
explanation.definitionFit: To plunder is to rob or loot goods by force.

clue.text: Admit a glacier could be transformed by this snapper

indicators.note: something transformed has changed shape, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A photographer admits a glacier changes when caught on film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'snapper' could suggest a fish or a turtle; here it is something that takes snaps.
explanation.definitionFit: A snapper is a camera or photographer; a digital model records images electronically.

clue.text: One mixes ingredients, for instance, less than UK consumer

indicators.note: the example abbreviation comes before, so it stands to the left of the rest

parts.note: e.g. is short for exempli gratia, for instance
GB, Great Britain, stands for the UK
an eater consumes food

explanation.surface: A puzzled comparison of a kitchen gadget with a British shopper.
explanation.definitionFit: An eggbeater is a hand whisk used to blend eggs and other foods.

clue.text: Coming from abroad, her enthusiastic follower

indicators.note: Coming from says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A keen fan arrives from overseas.
explanation.definitionFit: An adherent is a supporter or disciple of a cause or leader.

clue.text: Sad, cancelling recruitment?

definitions.meaning: sad in the sense of pitiful or letting one down

explanation.definitionFit: Disappointing means falling short of hopes, a let-down; split, it could mean un-hiring someone.

clue.text: Marches in street to keep needy uplifted

indicators.note: in a down clue uplifted means written upwards, so read backwards
to keep means to hold inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: the needy are poor

explanation.surface: Protest marches in the street to support the poor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uplifted' reverses SPOORT, the container built first.
explanation.definitionFit: To troop is to walk along in a group, as soldiers march.

clue.text: Call for dog to follow directions

indicators.note: to follow says the dog word comes after the compass letters

parts.note: E and N are the compass points east and north
to dog someone is to tail them

explanation.surface: Someone calls their dog to come along behind as they give directions.
explanation.definitionFit: To entail is to necessitate or require, as one thing calls for another.

clue.text: What makes a woman sparkle and occasionally strip abroad?

indicators.note: occasionally means every so often, so alternate letters are taken

explanation.surface: A cheeky question about what livens a woman up, including stripping on holiday.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiara is a jewelled headpiece that glitters on the wearer.

clue.text: Animal pelt expensive, we hear

indicators.note: we hear says the words are said aloud and spelt as another word

parts.note: to pelt down is to rain heavily; something expensive is dear

explanation.surface: An animal's fur costs a lot, people say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pelt' looks like fur, which suits the surface, but it is the verb meaning to pour with rain.
explanation.definitionFit: The reindeer is an Arctic deer, a large mammal.

clue.text: Some who might squeal over celebrity

indicators.note: over means turned over, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: rats are informers who squeal to the police, and also animals that squeak

explanation.surface: Informers telling tales about a famous person.
explanation.definitionFit: A star is a famous performer, a celebrity.

clue.text: Mrs Peron refurbished a cute retreat

parts.note: Eva Peron was the wife of Argentine president Juan Peron

indicators.note: refurbished means done over, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Evita does up a charming little hideaway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retreat' looks like a noun for the hideaway, but it is the verb, to withdraw.
explanation.definitionFit: To evacuate is to leave or withdraw from a place, as an army retreats.

clue.text: Display of arms?

parts.note: a military show featuring weapons, or an inked picture shown on someone's arm

explanation.walkthrough: A military tattoo is a display by armed forces, such as the Edinburgh Military Tattoo; arms are also limbs that bear ink.
explanation.definitionFit: A tattoo is both a military pageant and a design inked into skin.

clue.text: Tornado raging around France, first one way then the other

definitions.text: first one way then the other

indicators.note: around means the shuffled letters go round the next piece
a raging storm is wild and disordered, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: F is the international vehicle code for France

explanation.surface: A storm swirls across France, lurching back and forth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raging' turns TORNADO into TOANDRO, and 'around' puts that round F.
explanation.definitionFit: To and fro describes movement back and forth in alternating directions.

clue.text: Avoids satires about Republican

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece goes round the other

parts.note: skits are short satirical sketches

explanation.surface: A politician dodges comedy sketches mocking a Republican.
explanation.definitionFit: To skirt something is to go round its edge rather than through it, so to evade it.
